messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun was eight years old the first time he saw his father strike his mother. He remembered the sound—the flat crack of an open palm against her cheek—and the silence that followed, heavier than the blow. He had frozen in the doorway, his small body unwilling to move, his voice locked in his throat. No one came. No one ever came. His father faced no consequences; neighbors pretended not to hear, and his mother never spoke of it. Arjun grew up believing that the world was a place where bad things happened without anyone stepping in, and that he was powerless to stop them.

Now thirty-six and an accountant for a mid-sized firm in Chicago, Arjun lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment, five years divorced. He spends most of his days in a cubicle, hunched over spreadsheets, grateful for the quiet. But the quiet is never safe. Without warning, a coworker’s raised voice across the hall—someone laughing too loudly—can hurl him back into that doorway. The memory returns not as a story he can tell, but as a visceral crash: the smell of his mother’s perfume, the sting of his own held breath, the terror pouring through him like ice water. He cannot put it into words. He only feels it, and his body does what it learned to do: his heart pounds, his palms sweat, his muscles coil as if an attack is coming.

That feeling of constant threat has become the wallpaper of his life. Arjun’s body stays tense, ready to react to danger that rarely arrives. He scans every room for exits, every conversation for a shift in tone. He has come to believe that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will happen again. This hypervigilance, in turn, keeps the memories raw. Every sudden noise, every raised eyebrow, every moment of unexpected silence triggers without warning the same old terror, and he is eight years old again, watching helplessly.

The cycle tightens around him. Because the people who hurt his family never faced consequences, Arjun is certain that nothing he does matters. He used to be a happy child, but now he is always miserable, convinced that bad things will happen no matter how carefully he lives. When a memory crashes in—unbidden, wordless—it confirms his helplessness. And when he feels his body tense and his mind race, he tells himself that he is right to be afraid, because the world is unforgiving. The conviction that the world was unforgiving kept pulling him back into the memory of that silence after the slap, as if the past itself had to prove him right.

These beliefs have shaped his daily life. He avoids social gatherings, declines team projects, and leaves the office the moment his shift ends. His marriage ended because his wife could no longer reach him; he spent evenings locked in himself, certain that opening up would only invite more pain. At work, he is known as competent but distant. He once panicked during a budget meeting when two colleagues argued over numbers; he fled to the restroom and stood shaking over the sink, unable to speak. That was the moment he began to wonder if something was seriously wrong.

What finally brought Arjun to therapy was a string of such incidents—one too many mornings waking with his fists clenched, one too many nights lying awake listening for sounds that were not there. He is exhausted. He is afraid that he will never feel safe, never trust his own body again. But what frightens him most is the idea that he will pass this on, that his own children—if he ever lets himself have them—will grow up in the same invisible fog. He came because he wants to stop the cycle, even if he is not sure how.
